Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
2026 Quality Program Executive Summary The Quality Program provides a formal process to measure and improve the Health Plan’s excellent quality ratings across all lines of business systematically and objectively. The Quality Program’s mission is to lead a dynamic and cross-functional quality program that demonstrates and drives excellence in quality and customer experience. In strategic alignment with the Enterprise 7 Block Strategy, the Quality Program has a specific focus on “improving member and community health.” In addition to its quality focus, the program strives to achieve affordability and growth in all membership populations. The Key elements of the Quality Program are aligned with regulatory requirements from the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), New York State Department of Health (NYSDOH), National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), and the National Quality Strategy visions. The quality program’s foundation is driven by an organization-wide improvement strategy, Quality Improvement Program Description, an annual quality improvement evaluation of performance, and an annual Quality Improvement Program Action Plan. To support improvement efforts, monthly measurement and reporting also exist to trend and forecast performance. Continued review of quality improvement activities requires ongoing: • Execution of member engagement tactics to close gaps in care and improve experience. • Advancement of the collection of clinical data through partnerships with health information exchanges. • Continual monitoring of strategic action plans for all lines of business, including the expansion of the Dual Eligible Special Needs Program population and a strong focus on Medicare Stars. • Implementation of additional Predictive Analytics with integration into Quality Stratification for multiple-gap outreach and outcomes. • Evaluate potential for additional Medicare Value Based Care (VBC) arrangements and/or new incentive programs to improve core quality metrics performance. • Aligned Health Equity regulations and strategies into Quality Program initiatives and outcome reporting. 2026 Quality Improvement Program Description The Program Description is a comprehensive document that describes the Health Plan’s quality governance structure, program scope, goals and objectives, and additional regulatory components, all which are inclusive of physical and behavioral health for all lines of business. The connection to external providers and community partnerships and a demonstration of a heightened focus on Health Equity is described within the program description. The Program Description incorporates all lines of business as well as NCQA Accreditation and addresses health outcome inequities by integrating the health equity corporate strategy. In alignment with the Quality Program vision, the program description demonstrates the organization-wide efforts in place to achieve and maintain nationally recognized excellence in health care quality for all member populations that drives mission and strategy aligned quality, affordability, and growth. The Quality Improvement (QI) Program provides a formal process to monitor, improve, and evaluate the quality, efficiency, affordability, safety, and effectiveness of care and service utilizing a cross-functional, integrated, and collaborative approach. 2025 Quality Improvement Program Evaluation The program evaluation reflects organizational outcomes from the 2025 Action Plan. As part of the quality program, this document highlights accomplishments, measurement outcomes, barriers, and next steps for each initiative. The information contained in the program evaluation is modeled after the Plan-Do-Study-Act methodology to demonstrate the process from strategic planning to tracking milestones, barriers, lessons learned, and future planning. All initiatives are regularly monitored with key stakeholders throughout the year. 2025 Program Evaluation highlights: Domain: Highlights: Corporate Scorecard Metrics • Our Corporate Scorecard Quality Rating Program met two of three scorecard measures, supported by multiple initiatives aimed at improving Medicare performance. While the Health Plan saw improvement across many Star measures, 58% of measure cut points increased— raising the bar and making it more challenging to achieve high scores. • Aligned financial value for Quality Ratings and Incentives totaled $220.4M across Stars, New York State (NYS), Federal Employee Program (FEP), and Health and Recovery Plan (HARP). o Medicare: Achieved 4 Stars for HMO, 3.5 Stars for PPO, and 4.5 Stars for PDP, with work underway to impact 2026 results. o Commercial: Met the NCQA rating goal of 4 Stars. o SafetyNet: Ranked 5th out of 12 in the NYS Medicaid incentive program, while HARP ranked #1 statewide. Quality Program Performance Assessment • Overall, 82% of Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set (HEDIS) measures improved or maintained benchmark position, representing a 3% increase over last year. Performance outpaced the control group by 4.4%, with preventive health measures outperforming by approximately 6%. Focused Effort measures—those supported by improvement teams— outperformed the control group by 17%, demonstrating the impact of targeted interventions. Advancing NCQA Accreditation • Evidence collection for Year 1 2025 is substantially complete, with final reviews underway. The program remains on track to meet all Year 1 requirements, ensuring a smooth transition into Year 2 activities for 2026. Additionally, the Medicare Utilization Management Corrective Action Plan was successfully closed, resulting in full accreditation across all lines of business. Health Equity • Health Equity Innovation Awards exceeded $3 million, funding programs in behavioral health, maternal health, social determinants of health, and chronic conditions. Engagement efforts with Black/African American Medicare members improved colorectal cancer screening rates—HMO cohorts increased by 3.36 percentage points, and PPO by 1.179 points. • The Health Plan also hosted Community-Based Organization (CBO) Summits with over 400 participants, strengthening local partnerships. • The Health Equity Ambassadors Program continues to grow, with Cohort 2 graduating in April 2025, Cohort 3 completing in September, and recruitment for Cohort 4 underway with 62 sign-ups. Duals Special Needs Program (D-SNP) Readiness • Significant progress includes launching the D-SNP Stars Steering Team, developing a 2025 projection report to guide 2026 strategies, and distributing the Health Outcomes Survey (HOS) to members for the first time. Results are expected mid-2026 and will inform upcoming interventions. Planning for 2026 Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (CAHPS) and HOS samples is underway, and preparations for the 2027 Model of Care have begun. Member Experience • Collaboration across Quality Programs, Customer Care, Healthcare Engagement, Marketing, and Customer Experience teams continued to drive organization-wide member engagement campaigns aimed at improving quality performance across all lines of business. • CAHPS remains a critical component of health plan quality ratings. In 2025, the Health Plan strengthened CAHPS performance by expanding member experience insights through new data sources, enhancing analytics dashboards, improving closed-loop survey processes, and aligning enterprise-wide training and strategies. Risk-based strategies and campaigns for Medicare members launched in Summer and Fall 2025 delivered measurable results: o Drug Plan Rating: +13 points among low-risk members. o Health Plan Rating: Live member engagement increased pulse survey scores by +1–2 points. • The Customer Experience team supported Medicare engagement through strategic communications and virtual events, which achieved high satisfaction scores post-event (CAHPS: 84.6% for health plan, 81.8% for drug plan). • Marketing initiatives focused on multi-channel engagement, risk-based outreach, and integrating member feedback into content strategy. Key efforts leveraged J.D. Power recognition and successfully navigated market disruptions: o J.D. Power accolade campaigns achieved 39% engagement rates, far exceeding industry averages (4%), and typical health plan rates (8%). • A reacquisition campaign addressed widespread Medicare plan cancellations for 2026, including SMS outreach via Relay, which delivered engagement well above industry standards. Provider Experience • Overall provider satisfaction reached 81%, an increase of five points from last year and exceeding our goal. Participation was the highest to date, with 822 surveys completed. • The ACQA Cayuga Area Partners pilot successfully connected with members due for Annual Care Visits, scheduling these patients within the next 12 months. Risk stratification reports were leveraged to prioritize outreach and ensure timely care. • In May 2025, the Health Plan hosted the Quality Summit, focusing on key areas such as fall prevention, diabetes A1C control, hypertension management, and eye exam compliance. Additionally, provider education trainings were completed in September 2025, emphasizing quality improvement initiatives and best practices. Quality Data Strategy • The primary goal of the Quality Data Strategy was to deliver deeper analytic insights, expand reporting capabilities, and improve alignment with customer needs. Key accomplishments include: • Reporting Enhancements o Integrated gap closure values into existing reports and launched enhanced provider reporting models incorporating Stars ratings. o Developed dynamic “Star Measure” tools combining HEDIS, CAHPS, and Acumen adherence for comprehensive performance evaluation. o Added Medicare Annual Care Visit (MACV) measures to dashboards and created composite measures for annual physicals and wellness visits. • Data Infrastructure & Analytics o Initiated the Quality Data Foundations framework and integrated Acumen data into HEDIS dashboards for improved provider insights. o Built forecasting models for High Value Outreach teams to analyze call volume and efficiency. o Established predictive analytics feeding into member touchpoint repositories for engagement tracking. • Population & Compliance Analysis o Conducted Medicare persona analysis, Health Outcomes Survey follow-ups, and social risk factor studies, showing year-over-year improvement in HEDIS compliance. o Identified provider continuity as a key driver of compliance through spousal loss and provider termination studies. o WellBe and Emcara analyses confirmed higher compliance among engaged members. • Vendor Partnerships o Advanced reporting for WellBe and Vatica programs, including development of Vatica scorecards for gap closure measurement. o Explored partnerships targeting kidney health and obesity populations for 2026. • These efforts resulted in improved turnaround times for member claim utilization and Annual Care Visit (ACV) reporting. While Health Equity Index reporting was paused due to Medicare product changes, membership monitoring continues. The D-SNP case management pilot faced challenges due to frequent member enrollment and disenrollment. Gap Closure Strategy • Throughout 2025, predictive analytics continued to play a critical role in identifying gaps in care—over 575,000 gaps were flagged, including colorectal, breast, and cervical cancer screenings; blood pressure control; well-child visits; and eye and kidney screenings for members with diabetes. • Quality Programs Outreach campaigns directly engaged more than 595,000 members about their open gaps in care—a 200% increase since the mid-year assessment. The largest gains came from Predictive Mail and Email Campaigns, along with the addition of the Controlling Blood Pressure campaign in July. • The High Value Outreach (HVO) team expanded its community impact by supporting the Smile Mobile, starting with 7 events in August and growing to 25 events. These efforts provided Medicaid Managed Care members with access to dental care—many for the first time—and included targeted outreach to Spanish-speaking members to reduce language barriers. • HVO also supported Mobile Mammography initiatives, successfully scheduling Medicare and Medicaid Managed Care members for breast cancer screenings throughout the year Quality Program (QP) Enhancements - QP Governance and Socialization • The QP Governance team focused on executing an enhanced governance structure and improving communication and socialization of QP information across the entire organization, to members, providers, and communities across all regions. • The 2025 Quality Week campaign was executed in October in partnership with Capital District Physicians’ Health Plan (CDPHP), emphasizing gap closure and quality roles. SharePoint engagement was a key communication during 2025 and increased visibility through blog posts, communication campaigns, and committee presentations. o Over 1,026 unique views and nearly 8,000 total page views in 2025 (86% of all unique views since inception). o Quality Week content received 500+ blog views. NYS Strategy • The NYS Measurement Year (MY) 2023 results demonstrated significant progress. The HARP program achieved a #1 ranking, improving from #6 the previous year, and secured 100% of the program’s available funding—an estimated $3 million returned to the 2025 budget. Medicaid maintained a strong position at #5, while the Essential Plan advanced from #7 to #5, earning five bonus points. • The Quality team completed comprehensive annual Line of Business (LOB) strategies, including a new provider-aligned approach and deep-dive analysis of individual county data. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Office for Civil Rights (OCR) announced a settlement with Deer Oaks – The Behavioral Health Solution, resolving potential violations of the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules. Deer Oaks, a provider of psychological and psychiatric services to residents of long-term care and assisted living facilities, was investigated after two incidents: First, a complaint in May 2023 revealed that Deer Oaks impermissibly disclosed the ePHI of 35 individuals (including names, dates of birth, diagnoses) by making patient discharge summaries publicly accessible online due to a coding error in a discontinued pilot program (data exposed from at least December 2021 to May 19, 2023). OCR found that Deer Oaks failed to conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis as required by the HIPAA Security Rule. Under the settlement, Deer Oaks paid $225,000 and agreed to a two-year corrective action plan monitored by OCR to ensure compliance.

This article from Ogletree Deakins, authored by Benjamin W. Perry and Lauren N. Watson, analyzes 2025 HIPAA enforcement trends by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR). In the first five months of 2025, OCR announced ten HIPAA resolution agreements with covered entities and business associates—ranging from small physician groups to large hospital authorities and IT service providers—spanning both the Biden and Trump administrations. The common thread across all enforcement actions was the organizations' failure to conduct a thorough risk analysis consistent with the HIPAA Security Rule.

The underlying data breaches varied: ransomware attacks (e.g., a New York neurology practice and a Guam public hospital), phishing schemes (e.g., a California health network with nearly 200,000 individuals' records exposed), and ePHI left unsecured on internet-facing servers. In every case, OCR found the entity had not performed an enterprise-wide risk analysis.

Penalties were significant, with civil monetary fines ranging from $25,000 to $3,000,000 (the latter for a national medical supplier that failed to conduct a compliant risk analysis and suffered a phishing-related breach). Resolution agreements also included corrective action plans requiring completion of risk analyses, implementation of risk management plans, staff training, and security policy updates, often with multi-year HHS oversight.

The article emphasizes that OCR's 2025 enforcement actions make clear that HIPAA risk analysis is not an optional or "check-the-box" exercise but a critical compliance step. The authors advise healthcare organizations and their service providers to proactively prioritize regular risk analyses and security improvements to avoid regulatory scrutiny and financial consequences.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Top Five HIPAA Lessons Learned: A Review of HHS Resolution ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7839657

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Innovations in Clinical Neuroscience (2020) by Justin Pope, JD, reviews U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office of Civil Rights (OCR) HIPAA case resolution agreements to identify five key lessons for covered entities. The article notes that OCR enforcement has not slowed during the pandemic.

**Top Five HIPAA Lessons Learned:**

1. **A thorough, accurate, and current risk assessment is essential.** The Security Rule requires covered entities to assess risks, weigh threats/vulnerabilities, and implement policies accordingly. Notable cases: North Memorial Health Care ($1.55M settlement, stolen unencrypted laptop, no BAA, failed risk analysis); University of Washington Medicine ($750K settlement, malware accessed ePHI of 90,000, failed to ensure all affiliates conducted risk assessments).

2. **Devices storing ePHI should be encrypted and password-protected.** Over a third of OCR resolutions involve theft/loss of unencrypted portable devices. Encryption acts as a safe harbor—a lost encrypted device is not presumed a breach. Notable cases: Lifespan Health System ($1.04M, stolen unencrypted laptop); University of Rochester Medical Center ($3M, unencrypted flash drive and laptop); Feinstein Institute for Medical Research ($3.9M, stolen unencrypted laptop, 13,000 individuals affected).

3. **Get the Business Associate Agreement (BAA)!** Covered entities must have a BAA before disclosing PHI to any third party. Notable cases: Advanced Care Hospitalists PL ($500K, no BAA with billing vendor, PHI of 9,000 publicly viewable); Center for Children's Digestive Health ($31K, no BAA with FileFax); Pagosa Springs Medical Center ($111,400, no BAA with web-based scheduling vendor).

4. **Covered entities are responsible for the actions of their employees.** Providers must be vigilant with training, policies, and audit trails. Notable cases: St. Luke's-Roosevelt Hospital ($387,200, staff faxed PHI to wrong recipient); Memorial Healthcare System ($5.5M, former employee's credentials used to access ePHI of 80,000 individuals undetected for a year); UCLA Health System ($865,500, employees improperly accessed celebrity patients' ePHI).

5. **HIPAA compliance is an ongoing, dynamic process.** Policies must be reviewed and updated regularly. Notable cases: Woman & Infants Hospital of Rhode Island ($400K, failed to update BAA per Omnibus Rule); Anchorage Community Mental Health Services ($150K, policies no longer being followed, outdated software).

The article concludes that OCR continues to enforce HIPAA violations even during the pandemic, and covered entities should be proactive about confidentiality and security of health information.
</summary>

OCR prefers settlements over civil monetary penalties, and corrective action plans are typically included in settlements. ## Summary: What is a 'Corrective Action Plan' (CAP) in HIPAA?

This article from Abyde explains that HIPAA violation settlements involve more than just monetary fines — they often include a **Corrective Action Plan (CAP)**, which is a 1-2 year administrative oversight period requiring the violating practice to fix the issues that led to the breach.

### Key Requirements of a CAP (over 1-2 years):
- Report regularly to the Office for Civil Rights (OCR)
- Implement missing HIPAA policies (e.g., business associate agreements, employee training)
- Conduct a Security Risk Analysis (SRA) or a new one
- Develop a risk management plan
- Complete regular paperwork reporting progress
- Submit to additional audits to ensure compliance progress

### Consequences of Non-Compliance with CAP:
- Failing to complete a CAP can void the initial settlement
- Leaves the practice open to additional fines and penalties
- Practices must juggle CAP requirements on top of patient care, operations, and reputation management

### Related Recent HIPAA Settlements (as of August 2026):
1. **OSF Healthcare System** (Aug 2026): $552,250 fine + 2-year CAP. Ransomware attack exposed 53,000+ records. Missing SRA and delayed breach notification (5+ months).

- The OCR fines organizations not just for breaches, but for being ill-prepared (missing SRAs, insufficient policies, lack of training).

## Overview

This is the **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) Annual Report to Congress on Breaches of Unsecured Protected Health Information (PHI) for Calendar Year 2024**, as required by the HITECH Act.

## Key Statistics

- **OCR received 663 breach notifications affecting 500+ individuals** in 2024, a **9% decrease** from 2023, affecting approximately **242,908,056 individuals**.

## Breach Types (500+ Individuals)

1. **Hacking/IT incidents**: 81% of reports (534 reports), affecting 241,582,022 individuals (99% of affected individuals). The largest single breach involved approximately **192,000,000 individuals** from a ransomware attack on a healthcare clearinghouse.
2. **Unauthorized access or disclosure**: 16% of reports (108 reports), affecting 1,256,501 individuals.
3. **Theft**: 2% (16 reports), affecting 54,500 individuals.
4. **Improper disposal**: 3 reports, affecting 9,809 individuals.
5. **Loss**: 2 reports, affecting 5,224 individuals.

## Breach Locations (500+ Individuals)

- **Network server**: 63% of reports, 98% of affected individuals
- **Email**: 25% of reports
- **Paper records**: 5% of reports

- **Business associates**: 16% of reports (106 reports), **85% of affected individuals**
- **Health plans**: 8% of reports (50 reports), 1% of affected individuals
- **Health care clearinghouses**: <1% of reports

- **Loss**: 4% (2,593 reports)

- Most common location: **Paper records** (60% of reports)

## Key HIPAA Compliance Issues Identified

OCR identified these **Security Rule standards** needing improvement:
1. **Risk Analysis** – Incomplete assessments of risks to ePHI
2. **Risk Management** – Failure to implement sufficient security measures (e.g., multi-factor authentication)
3. **Information System Activity Review** – Infrequent or absence of regular review of audit logs
4. **Access Control** – Insufficient controls preventing unauthorized network access
5. **Person or Entity Authentication** – Weak passwords, single-factor remote access, compromised credentials

- **Plastic Surgery Associates of South Dakota**: $500,000 settlement for ransomware affecting 10,229 individuals
- **Providence Medical Institute**: $240,000 civil money penalty

Hacking/IT incidents remain the dominant threat to PHI, and OCR emphasizes the need for regulated entities to improve compliance with HIPAA Rules, particularly around risk analysis, risk management, and authentication controls.

<summary>
## Summary: What is a 'Corrective Action Plan' (CAP) in HIPAA?

This article from Abyde explains that HIPAA violation settlements involve more than just monetary fines — they often include a **Corrective Action Plan (CAP)**, which is a 1-2 year administrative oversight period requiring the violating practice to fix the issues that led to the breach.

### Key Requirements of a CAP (over 1-2 years):
- Report regularly to the Office for Civil Rights (OCR)
- Implement missing HIPAA policies (e.g., business associate agreements, employee training)
- Conduct a Security Risk Analysis (SRA) or a new one
- Develop a risk management plan
- Complete regular paperwork reporting progress
- Submit to additional audits to ensure compliance progress

### Consequences of Non-Compliance with CAP:
- Failing to complete a CAP can void the initial settlement
- Leaves the practice open to additional fines and penalties
- Practices must juggle CAP requirements on top of patient care, operations, and reputation management

### Related Recent HIPAA Settlements (as of August 2026):
1. **OSF Healthcare System** (Aug 2026): $552,250 fine + 2-year CAP. Ransomware attack exposed 53,000+ records. Missing SRA and delayed breach notification (5+ months).

   - **SG Health Plan** (employee benefit plan): $245,000 + 2-year CAP (9,316 members; no extensive SRA)

### Key Takeaways:
- The OCR fines organizations not just for breaches, but for being ill-prepared (missing SRAs, insufficient policies, lack of training).

## Overview

This is the **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) Annual Report to Congress on Breaches of Unsecured Protected Health Information (PHI) for Calendar Year 2024**, as required by the HITECH Act.

## Key Statistics

- **OCR received 663 breach notifications affecting 500+ individuals** in 2024, a **9% decrease** from 2023, affecting approximately **242,908,056 individuals**.
- **OCR received 74,299 breach reports affecting fewer than 500 individuals**, affecting **340,618 individuals** total.
- Between 2020 and 2024, breaches affecting fewer than 500 individuals increased by **12%**, while breaches affecting 500+ individuals rose by **1%**.
- OCR resolved **12 breach investigations** with resolution agreements, corrective action plans, and monetary settlements totaling **$7,813,831**.

## Breach Types (500+ Individuals)

1. **Hacking/IT incidents**: 81% of reports (534 reports), affecting 241,582,022 individuals (99% of affected individuals). The largest single breach involved approximately **192,000,000 individuals** from a ransomware attack on a healthcare clearinghouse.
2. **Unauthorized access or disclosure**: 16% of reports (108 reports), affecting 1,256,501 individuals.
3. **Theft**: 2% (16 reports), affecting 54,500 individuals.
4. **Improper disposal**: 3 reports, affecting 9,809 individuals.
5. **Loss**: 2 reports, affecting 5,224 individuals.

## Breach Locations (500+ Individuals)

- **Network server**: 63% of reports, 98% of affected individuals
- **Email**: 25% of reports
- **Paper records**: 5% of reports
- Other: Electronic medical records, laptops, portable devices, desktop computers

## Breaches by Entity Type (500+ Individuals)

- **Health care providers**: 76% of reports (505 reports), 14% of affected individuals
- **Business associates**: 16% of reports (106 reports), **85% of affected individuals**
- **Health plans**: 8% of reports (50 reports), 1% of affected individuals
- **Health care clearinghouses**: <1% of reports

## Breaches Affecting Fewer than 500 Individuals

- **Unauthorized access or disclosure**: 94% of reports (69,773 reports)
- **Loss**: 4% (2,593 reports)
- **Hacking/IT incidents**: 1% (885 reports)
- Majority from **health care providers** (93% of reports)
- Most common location: **Paper records** (60% of reports)

## Key HIPAA Compliance Issues Identified

OCR identified these **Security Rule standards** needing improvement:
1. **Risk Analysis** – Incomplete assessments of risks to ePHI
2. **Risk Management** – Failure to implement sufficient security measures (e.g., multi-factor authentication)
3. **Information System Activity Review** – Infrequent or absence of regular review of audit logs
4. **Access Control** – Insufficient controls preventing unauthorized network access
5. **Person or Entity Authentication** – Weak passwords, single-factor remote access, compromised credentials

## Enforcement Actions

OCR resolved 785 breach investigations through technical assistance, corrective action, or after determining no violation. Notable cases include:
- **Plastic Surgery Associates of South Dakota**: $500,000 settlement for ransomware affecting 10,229 individuals
- **Providence Medical Institute**: $240,000 civil money penalty

## Conclusion

Hacking/IT incidents remain the dominant threat to PHI, and OCR emphasizes the need for regulated entities to improve compliance with HIPAA Rules, particularly around risk analysis, risk management, and authentication controls.

URL: https://www.hhs.gov/about/agencies/dab/decisions/alj-decisions/2023/alj-cr6232/index.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Department of Health and Human Services Departmental Appeals Board Civil Remedies Division decision (DAB CR6232, February 16, 2023) regarding a HIPAA Privacy Rule enforcement action against Phoenix Healthcare, LLC d/b/a Green Country Care Center, a skilled nursing facility in Tulsa, Oklahoma.

**Key Facts:**
- On March 13, 2019, the complainant (daughter of a former resident) requested a copy of the affected party's medical records.
- The facility's business associate (Secrest, Hill, Butler & Secrest law firm) demanded $467.50 (50 cents/page based on Oklahoma state law) for hard copies, later offering electronic copies for $200.
- Neither fee was "reasonable and cost-based" as required by HIPAA (45 C.F.R. § 164.524).
- The complainant refused to pay, and the records were not provided until January 30, 2020 — over 10 months after the request.
- The facility did not have a written business associate agreement with the Secrest firm until September 20, 2019, despite the firm serving as business associate for nearly 20 years.

**Violations Found:**
1. Failure to provide timely access to the designated record set (willful neglect tier), from May 30, 2019 through January 29, 2020.
2. Charging a fee that contravened 45 C.F.R. § 164.524 (willful neglect tier), for a single day on July 1, 2019.
3. Failure to have a written business associate agreement (reasonable cause tier), from March 30, 2015 through September 19, 2019.

**Penalty:**
- OCR calculated total CMP liability at $4,071,131 but proposed a reduced CMP of $250,000 based on claimed financial hardship and COVID-19 impact.
- The ALJ upheld the violations but reduced the CMP to $75,000 based on evaluation of the 45 C.F.R. § 160.408 factors.

**Procedural History:**
- OCR opened investigation after the complainant filed complaints in April and May 2019.
- Despite OCR's April 30, 2019 letter explaining HIPAA fee requirements, Respondent continued to demand inflated fees.
- Respondent (through the Secrest firm) engaged in protracted litigation, including baseless arguments about the entity's identity and conflicts of interest.
- The Secrest firm withdrew from representation in February 2022 after the ALJ raised conflict concerns.
- Respondent conceded the proper entity was "Phoenix Healthcare, LLC d/b/a Green Country Care Center" in April 2022.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"OCR determined that the total civil monetary penalty (CMP) for which Respondent was liable was $4,071,131, but proposed a CMP of $250,000 based on its evaluation of the factors listed in 45 C.F.R. § 160.408.", "I uphold OCR's determination that Respondent committed the aforementioned violations of the Privacy Rule, along with OCR's determinations regarding Respondent's level of culpability for each violation and the duration of each violation. However, based on an evaluation of the factors listed at 45 C.F.R. § 160.408, a CMP of $75,000 is justified.", "Willful neglect, pursuant to 45 C.F.R. § 160.401, is defined as the 'conscious, intentional failure or reckless indifference to the obligation to comply with the administrative simplification provision violated.'", "By conditioning its fulfillment of the records request on either payment of $467.50 (for a hard copy) or $200 (for an electronic copy), which the complainant was unwilling to pay because the amounts were not reasonable and cost-based, Respondent did not provide the requested records."

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### I. Overview of HIPAA Resolution Agreements and Corrective Action Plans

According to HHS.gov, a resolution agreement is a settlement agreement signed by HHS and a covered entity or business associate in which the covered entity or business associate agrees to perform certain obligations and make reports to HHS, generally for a period of three years. During the period, HHS monitors the covered entity's compliance with its obligations. A resolution agreement may include the payment of a resolution amount. If HHS cannot reach a satisfactory resolution through the covered entity's demonstrated compliance or corrective action through other informal means, including a resolution agreement, civil money penalties (CMPs) may be imposed for noncompliance against a covered entity. [Source 5]

According to the Compliancy Group, when the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) determines a covered entity or business associate has violated HIPAA, OCR may impose a CAP to correct underlying privacy and security compliance issues, in addition to fines. The CAP typically requires closely-monitored security risk analyses and risk management plans. In extreme cases, OCR may require hiring a third-party monitor at the entity's expense. CAPs can span one to several years, requiring regular reports to OCR and audits. Failure to comply with a CAP is considered a breach of the resolution agreement and can lead to additional penalties. Specific measures may include: developing/revising policies and procedures for HHS approval; providing training materials on fulfilling rights of access requests; and submitting written reports to HHS by deadlines (e.g., 60 days) and annually until the CAP ends. [Source 15]

According to Abyde, a Corrective Action Plan (CAP) is basically equivalent to "you messed up, here's two years of administrative paperwork to fix your issues and think about what you've done." Failing to complete a corrective action plan within the designated time frame can void the initial settlement and can leave a practice open to additional fines and penalties. Key requirements of a CAP (over 1-2 years) include: Report regularly to the Office for Civil Rights (OCR); Implement missing HIPAA policies (e.g., business associate agreements, employee training); Conduct a Security Risk Analysis (SRA) or a new one; Develop a risk management plan; Complete regular paperwork reporting progress; Submit to additional audits to ensure compliance progress. [Source 14]

According to the HIPAA Journal, OCR prefers to settle alleged HIPAA violations rather than pursue civil monetary penalties. Civil monetary penalties require more resources, and when a civil monetary penalty is imposed, OCR cannot compel a HIPAA-regulated entity to adopt a corrective action plan. [Source 20]

---

### II. High-Penalty Cases ($1M+) from August 2021 to August 2026

#### Case 1: Excellus Health Plan – $5.1 Million Settlement (January 2021)

**Note:** This case was settled in January 2021, approximately 7 months before the August 2021 start date specified, but it is included as it is the closest high-penalty case and its CAP requirements are highly informative.

According to HHS.gov, Excellus Health Plan (doing business as Excellus BlueCross BlueShield, Univera Healthcare, and others) agreed to pay $5.1 million to the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) and to implement a corrective action plan to settle potential violations of the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules related to a breach affecting over 9.3 million people. Excellus Health Plan is a New York state health services corporation that provides health insurance coverage to over 1.5 million people in Upstate and Western New York. [Source 15]

According to the HIPAA Journal, the breach was discovered in August 2015, with hackers having gained access to Excellus's computer systems from approximately December 23, 2013, through May 11, 2015. The attackers installed malware, performed reconnaissance, and accessed healthcare data including names, contact information, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, health plan ID numbers, claims data, financial account information, and clinical treatment information. [Source 14]

OCR's investigation identified five areas of potential noncompliance with HIPAA Rules, including:
- Failure to conduct an accurate and thorough organization-wide risk analysis
- Insufficient measures to reduce risks and vulnerabilities to ePHI
- Inadequate technical policies and procedures for controlling access to systems containing ePHI
- Lack of policies and procedures requiring regular reviews of information system activity [Source 14]

According to Frier Levitt, OCR revealed that Excellus may have failed to conduct enterprise-wide risk analysis, and failed to implement risk management, information system activity review, and access controls. [Source 12]

The settlement was reached without admission of liability. Excellus must also adopt a corrective action plan and will be monitored by OCR for 2 years. [Source 14]

OCR Director Roger Severino commented on the case, noting that "hacking continues to be the greatest threat to the privacy and security of individuals' health information. In this case, a health plan did not stop hackers from roaming inside its health record system undetected for over a year which endangered the privacy of millions of its beneficiaries," and that "We know that the most dangerous hackers are sophisticated, patient, and persistent. Health care entities need to step up their game to protect the privacy of people's health information from this growing threat." [Source 14]

---

#### Case 2: L.A. Care Health Plan – $1.3 Million Settlement (September 2023)

According to the HHS.gov resolution agreement page, the Resolution Agreement and Corrective Action Plan (CAP) between HHS Office for Civil Rights and L.A. Care Health Plan (LACHP) was dated July 28, 2023 (LACHP) and August 1, 2023 (HHS). The agreement stems from two HIPAA privacy breach incidents. [Source 18]

The first incident was a January 2014 breach where LACHP members could view other members' protected health information (PHI) through the member portal due to a manual information processing error (less than 500 individuals affected). A breach report was filed February 26, 2016. The second incident was a January 2019 breach where a mailing error caused member ID cards to be sent to the wrong members, affecting approximately 1,498 individuals. Reported to OCR on March 15, 2019. [Source 18]

According to PAAS National, L.A. Care Health Plan (LACHP), the largest publicly operated health plan in the U.S., paid $1,300,000 to settle potential HIPAA Security Rule violations. The settlement stemmed from two OCR investigations: one involving a large data breach from a mailing error where member ID cards were sent to the wrong members, and another from a processing error that allowed members to potentially view other members' names, addresses, and member identification numbers on the payment portal. Beyond the settlement, LACHP agreed to a comprehensive corrective action plan and three years of OCR monitoring, including developing HIPAA compliance policies, performing risk analyses, and implementing risk management plans. [Source 11]

According to McGuireWoods, OCR alleged LA Care failed to conduct a risk analysis, implement sufficient security measures, regularly review system activity records, perform periodic evaluations in response to operational changes, and implement mechanisms to record and examine information system activity. The breaches occurred amid LA Care's expansion between 2014-2015, including adding 180,000 new members, launching a new online member portal, and increasing online access to health information. As part of the settlement, LA Care entered into a corrective action plan requiring an enterprise-wide risk analysis, HIPAA-specific policies and procedures, a risk management plan, and employee training. LA Care must submit annual compliance reports to OCR and may face civil monetary penalties for noncompliance. [Source 15]

According to the HHS.gov resolution agreement, the CAP compliance term is three years from the effective date. Key contacts include Thomas Mapp (Chief Compliance Officer), Serge Herrera (Privacy Officer), and Gene Magerr (Information Security Officer) for LACHP, and Steven Chen (Investigator) for HHS. LACHP must retain compliance-related documents for six years. [Source 18]

According to the HIPAA Journal, L.A. Care Health Plan settled without admitting liability, agreeing to pay a $1,300,000 penalty and adopt a corrective action plan requiring a comprehensive organization-wide risk analysis, risk management plan, development and distribution of related policies and procedures, reporting evaluations of environmental changes to OCR, and reporting employee HIPAA violations to OCR within 30 days. [Source 17]

According to Fierce Healthcare, under a corrective action plan, L.A. Care must create a risk management plan, conduct risk analyses, and report compliance failures to HHS within 30 days. [Source 16]

OCR Director Melanie Fontes Rainer stated: "Breaches of protected health information by a HIPAA-regulated entity often reveal systemic, noncompliance with the HIPAA Rules. HIPAA-regulated entities need to be proactive in ensuring their compliance with the HIPAA Rules, and not wait for OCR to reveal long-standing HIPAA deficiencies." [Source 17]

---

#### Case 3: Montefiore Medical Center – $4.75 Million Settlement (February 2024)

According to the HIPAA Journal, the $4.75 million HIPAA penalty was imposed on Montefiore Medical Center by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) in February 2024, stemming from a malicious insider incident. Between January and June 2013, an employee unlawfully accessed the medical records of 12,517 patients, copied their information, and sold it to identity thieves. The New York Police Department notified Montefiore in May 2015, and OCR was notified in July 2015. [Source 19]

OCR's investigation found multiple HIPAA Security Rule violations: failure to conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis of ePHI vulnerabilities, failure to implement procedures to review records of activity in information systems, and failure to implement hardware, software, or procedural mechanisms to record and examine activity in information systems. [Source 19]

According to Ankura, the settlement includes a $4.75 million civil monetary penalty and a corrective action plan with two years of OCR monitoring. OCR issued key recommendations for HIPAA-covered entities, including: reviewing vendor/contractor relationships and business associate agreements; integrating risk analysis and risk management into business processes; implementing audit controls; regularly reviewing information system activity; using multi-factor authentication; encrypting protected health information; incorporating lessons learned from past incidents; and providing regular, role-specific training. [Source 16]

According to McGuireWoods, as part of the $4.75 million settlement (without admitting liability), Montefiore agreed to a two-year Corrective Action Plan requiring a comprehensive security risk analysis, inventory of all facilities and systems containing ePHI, a risk management plan, audit controls, new policies and procedures, employee training, and reporting standards. [Source 18]

According to the HIPAA Journal, this was the largest financial penalty to be imposed by OCR since January 2021's $5.1 million penalty for Excellus Health Plan. Montefiore settled without admitting wrongdoing and agreed to a corrective action plan including conducting a risk assessment, developing a risk management plan, implementing audit controls, revising policies, and providing workforce training. OCR will monitor compliance for two years. [Source 19]

OCR Director Melanie Fontes Rainer stated: "Unfortunately, we are living in a time where cyber-attacks from malicious insiders are not uncommon. Now more than ever, the risks to patient protected health information cannot be overlooked and must be addressed swiftly and diligently." [Source 19]

---

#### Case 4: Solara Medical Supplies – $3 Million Settlement (December 2024)

According to the HHS.gov resolution agreement, the Resolution Agreement and Corrective Action Plan (CAP) between Solara Medical Supplies, LLC and the HHS Office for Civil Rights was dated December 11, 2024. The Compliance Term is two years from the Effective Date (December 11, 2024), with potential extension if a breach occurs. [Source 10]

According to TechTarget, the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) reached a $3 million settlement with Solara Medical Supplies, a supplier of diabetes patient supplies, to resolve potential HIPAA violations stemming from a 2019 phishing attack. Between April and June 2019, an unauthorized party gained access to eight employee email accounts, affecting over 114,000 individuals. Exposed data included names, addresses, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, patient login information, and diagnoses. [Source 6]

OCR's investigation uncovered several HIPAA violations, including failure to conduct a thorough risk assessment, failure to provide timely breach notifications to affected individuals, and failure to notify media outlets as required when a breach affects over 500 residents of a jurisdiction. Additionally, in January 2020, Solara filed a second breach report after sending 1,531 breach notification letters to wrong addresses. [Source 6]

According to the HHS.gov resolution agreement, the corrective actions required include: [Source 10]

**Risk Analysis:** Solara must conduct an enterprise-wide risk analysis of ePHI risks and vulnerabilities, including a complete inventory of all electronic equipment, data systems, and applications containing ePHI. The scope/methodology must be submitted within 90 days, and the full analysis within 180 days of HHS approval.

**Risk Management Plan:** Develop an enterprise-wide plan to address identified risks, with deadlines tied to HHS approval of the Risk Analysis.

**Policies and Procedures:** Develop/revise written policies to comply with HIPAA Privacy, Security, and Breach Notification Rules (45 C.F.R. Parts 160 and 164), with implementation deadlines.

**Training:** Augment HIPAA and Security Training Program, with training materials submitted to HHS for approval.

**Reportable Events:** Solara must report workforce member sanctions for policy violations within 30 days.

**Reporting:** Submit an Implementation Report within 120 days of training approval, plus Annual Reports for each year of the Compliance Term.

**Document Retention:** Maintain all compliance documents for 6 years from the Effective Date.

**Breach Provisions:** If Solara breaches the CAP, HHS may impose a Civil Monetary Penalty (CMP) under 45 C.F.R. Part 160. Solara has 60 days to cure or demonstrate compliance.

Signatories: Wendy Russalesi (Chief Compliance Officer, Solara) and Michael Leoz (Regional Manager, HHS Office for Civil Rights, Pacific Region). [Source 10]

According to Defensorum, Solara Medical Supplies violated 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) of the HIPAA Security Law when it did not perform a thorough and correct risk analysis to determine risks and vulnerabilities to the ePHI stored in its systems. Solara Medical Supplies did not issue prompt notifications to the HHS for the two breaches, did not give prompt notifications to the people impacted by the phishing breach, and failed to give prompt notification to leading media outlets regarding the phishing breach. Solara decided to a settlement including a payment of a $3,000,000 financial penalty and implementation of a corrective action plan that addresses all likely HIPAA violations. Solara separately resolved a class action lawsuit over the data breach by paying $9.76 million. [Source 7]

OCR Director Melanie Fontes Rainer stated: "Cyberattacks have skyrocketed exponentially in recent years. Effective cybersecurity requires identifying potential risks and vulnerabilities to health information and implementing effective security measures to protect against them. Health care entities that fail to address identified cybersecurity issues leave themselves vulnerable to cyberattacks. OCR urges health care entities to prioritize securing their information systems and take all necessary steps to reduce and prevent cyberattacks and safeguard protected health information." [Source 6]

#### Case 5: Warby Parker – $1.5 Million Civil Money Penalty (2025)

**Note:** This case involved a civil monetary penalty (CMP), not a settlement with a CAP. According to the HIPAA Journal, OCR prefers to settle alleged HIPAA violations rather than pursue civil monetary penalties. When a civil monetary penalty is imposed, OCR cannot compel a HIPAA-regulated entity to adopt a corrective action plan. [Source 20]

According to the HIPAA Journal, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) imposed its first financial penalty under the Trump administration for HIPAA noncompliance on Warby Parker, Inc., a manufacturer and online retailer of prescription and non-prescription eyewear. Warby Parker must pay a $1.5 million civil monetary penalty to resolve alleged HIPAA Rule violations. [Source 23]

The penalty stems from a credential stuffing attack that occurred between September 25, 2018, and November 30, 2018, where hackers accessed customer accounts via Warby Parker's website using usernames and passwords obtained from a data breach at an unrelated entity. Warby Parker initially reported the breach in December 2018, and later updated it on September 18, 2020, to 197,986 affected individuals. Compromised data included names, addresses, email addresses, last four digits of payment card information, and eyewear prescription information. Separate breach reports filed in September 2019, January 2020, April 2020, and June 2022 involved credential stuffing attacks affecting 484 additional individuals. [Source 23]

OCR's investigation, which began on September 16, 2019, found Warby Parker violated multiple HIPAA provisions: failing to conduct an accurate and comprehensive risk analysis to identify risks and vulnerabilities to ePHI, insufficient security measures to reduce risks, and failure to implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity. Warby Parker was given an opportunity to settle informally on March 14, 2024, but declined. OCR determined that evidence of recognized security practices did not adequately demonstrate they had been in place for 12 months prior to the breach, so the penalty was not reduced. No corrective action plan was imposed, as CAPs are only agreed upon in informal settlements. [Source 23]

OCR Acting Director Anthony Archeval stated: "Identifying and addressing potential risks and vulnerabilities to electronic protected health information is necessary for effective cybersecurity and compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule. Protecting individuals' electronic health information means regulated entities need to be vigilant in implementing and complying with the Security Rule requirements before they experience a breach." [Source 23]

According to Abyde, Warby Parker was fined $1.5 million by the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) for HIPAA violations stemming from a series of credential stuffing cyberattacks that began in late 2018 and continued through 2022, impacting nearly 200,000 patients. The OCR investigation found that Warby Parker failed to conduct an adequate Security Risk Analysis (SRA), implement sufficient technical safeguards, or regularly review system access. In 2025, the OCR has issued over $5 million in fines so far, almost all of which involved a missing Security Risk Analysis (SRA). [Source 21]

#### Case 6: Gulf Coast Pain Consultants – $1.19 Million Civil Money Penalty (December 2024)

**Note:** This case involved a civil monetary penalty (CMP), not a settlement with a CAP.

According to the HIPAA Journal, on December 4, 2024, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) imposed a $1.19 million civil monetary penalty on Gulf Coast Pain Consultants, LLC (doing business as Clearway Pain Solutions Institute), a Florida-based pain management practice with locations in multiple states, for failing to terminate former workforce members' access to systems containing electronic protected health information (ePHI) and other HIPAA Security Rule violations. [Source 5]

The case stemmed from an incident involving an independent contractor engaged for business consulting services from May 2018. The contractor stopped providing services in August 2018, but their access was not terminated. Between September 7, 2018, and February 3, 2019, the contractor accessed the electronic medical record system without authorization on three occasions, exposing the ePHI of approximately 34,310 individuals (names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, chart numbers, insurance information, and primary care information). The contractor also generated around 6,500 false Medicare claims. [Source 5]

OCR's investigation revealed multiple compliance failures:
- The first HIPAA-compliant risk analysis was not conducted until September 30, 2022.
- Policies for reviewing activity in information systems containing ePHI were not implemented until April 10, 2020.
- Policies for terminating former workforce members' access to ePHI were first implemented on April 10, 2020.
- Policies for establishing, documenting, reviewing, and modifying users' right of access were first implemented on April 15, 2020. [Source 5]

Gulf Coast Pain Consultants was found to have violated 45 C.F.R. §164.308(a)(ii)(A), §164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D), §164.308(a)(3)(ii)(c), and §164.308(a)(4)(ii)(c) of the HIPAA Security Rule. This was the 14th HIPAA enforcement action of 2024 resulting in a financial penalty and OCR's 6th civil monetary penalty of the year. [Source 5]

According to Rivkin Radler, OCR's investigation found that the former contractor intended to obtain protected health information (PHI) for use in potential fraudulent Medicare claims. OCR concluded that Gulf Coast failed to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule which requires, among other things: (i) conducting thorough risk assessments; (ii) implementing procedures to regularly review records of activity; (iii) implementing procedures to terminate a workforce member's access; and (iv) implementing procedures for establishing and modifying workforce members' access. [Source 3]

OCR Director Melanie Fontes Rainer stated: "Current and former workforce can present threats to health care privacy and security—risking continuity of care and trust in our health care system. Effective cybersecurity and compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule means being proactive in reviewing who has access to health information and responding quickly to suspected security incidents." [Source 5]

The breach stemmed from a phishing email campaign that installed malware, giving attackers access to the insurer's IT system for nearly nine months undetected. This is the second-largest settlement in OCR's HIPAA enforcement history (largest: $16 million with Anthem involving 79 million individuals). [Source 10]

### III. Recurring Corrective Action Plan Requirements Across Multiple Cases

Based on the analysis of the high-penalty cases above, the following recurring CAP requirements have been identified:

#### 1. Mandatory Completion of a Thorough and Accurate Risk Analysis

This requirement appears in virtually every case. Key examples:

- **Excellus Health Plan (2021):** Failure to conduct an accurate and thorough organization-wide risk analysis was one of the primary violations. The CAP required an enterprise-wide risk analysis. [Source 14]
- **L.A. Care Health Plan (2023):** The CAP required a comprehensive organization-wide risk analysis. [Source 17]
- **Montefiore Medical Center (2024):** The CAP required a comprehensive security risk analysis including an inventory of all facilities and systems containing ePHI. [Source 18]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** The CAP specifically requires Solara to "conduct and complete an accurate, thorough, enterprise-wide analysis of risks and vulnerabilities that incorporates all risks to Solara's ePHI related to electronic equipment, data systems, programs, and applications." The scope/methodology must be submitted within 90 days, and the full analysis within 180 days of HHS approval. [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** The CAP requires risk analysis as a core component. [Source 10]
- **SG Health Plan (2026):** The CAP requires comprehensive risk analysis. [Source 9]
- **Elgon, Inc. (2024):** The CAP specifically requires implementing a security management process under 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(1)(i) & (ii) to address the failure to conduct an accurate and thorough risk assessment. [Source 4]

According to Ogletree Deakins, in the first five months of 2025, OCR announced ten HIPAA resolution agreements. The common thread across all enforcement actions was the organizations' failure to conduct a thorough risk analysis consistent with the HIPAA Security Rule. In every case, OCR found the entity had not performed an enterprise-wide risk analysis. The penalties assessed by OCR in 2025 for failing to do this ranged from as little as $25,000 at the low end to as much as $3 million for a national medical supplier that did not conduct a "compliant risk analysis" and subsequently suffered a major data breach after a phishing incident. [Source 3]

According to Feldesman, OCR's "Risk Analysis Initiative" was launched in fall 2024 and resulted in seven enforcement actions within its first six months against HIPAA-regulated entities for failing to conduct adequate security risk analyses. In every single case, OCR indicated that after their investigation, the regulated entities failed "to conduct an accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all its electronic PHI (ePHI). See 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)." [Source 6]

#### 2. Development and Implementation of Risk Management Plans

This requirement appears in nearly every CAP. Key examples:

- **L.A. Care Health Plan (2023):** The CAP required a risk management plan. [Source 17]
- **Montefiore Medical Center (2024):** The CAP required developing a risk management plan. [Source 19]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** The CAP requires Solara to "develop an enterprise-wide Risk Management Plan to address and mitigate any security risks and vulnerabilities identified in the Risk Analysis," with deadlines tied to HHS approval of the Risk Analysis. [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** The CAP requires risk management plan development. [Source 10]
- **SG Health Plan (2026):** The CAP requires a risk management plan. [Source 9]

#### 3. Revision and Implementation of HIPAA Privacy and Security Policies and Procedures

This requirement is standard across all CAPs. Key examples:

- **Excellus Health Plan (2021):** The CAP required revised policies and procedures. [Source 14]
- **L.A. Care Health Plan (2023):** The CAP required development and distribution of related policies and procedures. [Source 17]
- **Montefiore Medical Center (2024):** The CAP required new policies and procedures. [Source 18]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** The CAP requires Solara to "develop, maintain, and revise its written policies and procedures to comply with the Federal standards that govern the privacy and security of individually identifiable health information (45 C.F.R. Part 160 and Subparts A, C, D and E of Part 164, the Privacy Rule, Security Rule, and Breach Notification Rule)." [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** The CAP requires implementation of policies and procedures. [Source 10]
- **Elgon, Inc. (2024):** The CAP requires implementing a security management process. [Source 4]

#### 4. Workforce Training on HIPAA Policies and Procedures

This requirement is standard across all CAPs. Key examples:

- **L.A. Care Health Plan (2023):** The CAP required employee training. [Source 15]
- **Montefiore Medical Center (2024):** The CAP required employee training. [Source 18]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** The CAP requires Solara to "augment HIPAA and Security Training Program, with training materials submitted to HHS for approval." [Source 10]
- **Elgon, Inc. (2024):** The CAP requires providing security awareness and training for its workforce under 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(5). [Source 4]
- **SG Health Plan (2026):** The CAP requires training. [Source 9]

#### 5. Third-Party Monitoring or Independent Review/Monitoring by OCR

According to the Compliancy Group, in extreme cases, OCR may require hiring a third-party monitor at the entity's expense. [Source 15]

While third-party monitors are not always explicitly required, OCR monitoring is standard. Key examples:

- **L.A. Care Health Plan (2023):** Three years of OCR monitoring. [Source 11]
- **Montefiore Medical Center (2024):** Two years of OCR monitoring. [Source 16]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** Two years of OCR monitoring. [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** Two-year Compliance Term with OCR monitoring. [Source 10]
- **SG Health Plan (2026):** Two-year CAP with OCR monitoring. [Source 9]
- **Elgon, Inc. (2024):** Three-year Compliance Term. [Source 4]

#### 6. Submission of Compliance Reports to OCR (Implementation Reports and Annual Reports)

This requirement appears in virtually all CAPs. Key examples:

- **L.A. Care Health Plan (2023):** Must submit annual compliance reports to OCR. [Source 15]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** Must submit an Implementation Report within 120 days of training approval, plus Annual Reports for each year of the Compliance Term. [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** Must submit an Implementation Report within 120 days of HHS approval of policies, and Annual Reports within 60 days after each reporting period. [Source 10]
- **Elgon, Inc. (2024):** Must submit an Implementation Report and Annual Reports with attestations signed by an owner or officer confirming implementation of policies, workforce training completion, and accuracy of information. [Source 4]
- **SG Health Plan (2026):** Must submit Annual Reports. [Source 9]

#### 7. Reportable Events / Reporting of Security Incidents and Workforce Violations to OCR

This is a specific requirement in several CAPs. Key examples:

- **L.A. Care Health Plan (2023):** Must report employee HIPAA violations to OCR within 30 days. [Source 17] Must report compliance failures to HHS within 30 days. [Source 16]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** Must report workforce member sanctions for policy violations within 30 days ("Reportable Events"). [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** The agreement includes breach provisions with a 30-day cure period before HHS may impose civil money penalties. [Source 10]

#### 8. Specific Deadlines and Milestone Reporting Requirements

All CAPs include specific deadlines. Key examples:

- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** Risk analysis scope/methodology must be submitted within 90 days; full analysis within 180 days of HHS approval; Implementation Report within 120 days of training approval; Annual Reports within each year of Compliance Term. [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** Implementation Report within 120 days of HHS approval of policies; Annual Reports within 60 days after each reporting period. [Source 10]
- **Elgon, Inc. (2024):** Must submit Implementation Report and Annual Reports. [Source 4]

#### 9. Document Retention Requirements

Several CAPs include specific document retention periods. Key examples:

- **L.A. Care Health Plan (2023):** Must retain compliance-related documents for six years. [Source 18]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** Must maintain all compliance documents for 6 years from the Effective Date. [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** Document retention is required for six years from the Effective Date. [Source 10]
- **Elgon, Inc. (2024):** All documents and records relating to compliance must be retained for six (6) years from the Effective Date. [Source 4]
- **SG Health Plan (2026):** Document retention requirements for six (6) years from the Effective Date. [Source 9]

#### 10. Annual Certifications of Compliance by Entity Leadership

This is a specific requirement in several CAPs. Key examples:

- **Elgon, Inc. (2024):** Must submit Annual Reports with attestations signed by an owner or officer confirming implementation of policies, workforce training completion, and accuracy of information. [Source 4]
- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** The Implementation Report and Annual Reports are submitted to OCR, signed by leadership. [Source 10]

#### 11. Compliance Term Duration

The duration of CAPs varies. Key examples:
- **Two years:** Solara Medical Supplies (2024), Montefiore Medical Center (2024), Regional Women's Health Group (2025), SG Health Plan (2026), Assured Imaging (2026), Consociate Health (2026), RWHG (2026) [Sources 10, 19, 9, 14]
- **Three years:** L.A. Care Health Plan (2023), Excellus Health Plan (2021), Elgon, Inc. (2024), MMG Fusion (2026) [Sources 18, 14, 4, 12]

#### 12. Breach/Cure Provisions

Many CAPs include specific provisions regarding breach of the CAP. Key examples:

- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** If Solara breaches the CAP, HHS may impose a Civil Monetary Penalty (CMP) under 45 C.F.R. Part 160. Solara has 60 days to cure or demonstrate compliance. [Source 10]
- **Regional Women's Health Group (2025):** The agreement includes breach provisions with a 30-day cure period before HHS may impose civil money penalties. [Source 10]

According to Abyde, failing to complete a corrective action plan within the designated time frame can void the initial settlement and can leave a practice open to additional fines and penalties. [Source 14]

#### 13. Inventory of Systems and Assets Containing ePHI

Several CAPs specifically require a complete inventory. Key examples:

- **Solara Medical Supplies (2024):** Must include "a complete inventory of all electronic equipment, data systems, and applications containing ePHI" as part of the risk analysis. [Source 10]
- **Montefiore Medical Center (2024):** The CAP required an inventory of all facilities and systems containing ePHI. [Source 18]

#### 14. Audit Controls and Information System Activity Review

Several CAPs specifically require implementation of audit controls. Key examples:

- **Montefiore Medical Center (2024):** The CAP required implementing audit controls. [Source 19]
- **Premera Blue Cross (2020):** The CAP required revised policies covering access/audit controls. [Source 10]

#### A. L.A. Care Health Plan (2023) – Reporting Workforce Violations

The L.A. Care CAP had a particularly stringent requirement that the entity must report employee HIPAA violations to OCR within 30 days. [Source 17] Additionally, L.A. Care must report compliance failures to HHS within 30 days. [Source 16]
